solution: A collection is a set only if, for every object, it can be decided definitely whether the object belongs to the collection. Here the months beginning with the letter J are exactly January, June and July, and for any month one can decide at once whether its name begins with J. The collection is well defined, so it is a set, namely \(\{\text{January},\ \text{June},\ \text{July}\}\).

The word "talented" is a matter of opinion, so different people will name different writers and there is no rule that decides whether a given writer belongs to the collection. The collection is not well defined, so it is not a set.

"Best" is not a definite criterion; whether a particular batsman is among the eleven best is a matter of opinion and varies from person to person. The collection is not well defined, so it is not a set.
For any person one can decide definitely whether that person is a boy of your class. The collection is well defined, so it is a set.
For any object one can decide definitely whether it is a natural number smaller than \(100\); the collection is exactly \(\{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 99\}\). It is well defined, so it is a set.
Whether a given novel was written by Munshi Prem Chand is a definite fact, not a matter of opinion. The collection is well defined, so it is a set.
An integer \(x\) is even exactly when \(x = 2n\) for some integer \(n\), so for any object one can decide definitely whether it belongs to the collection. It is well defined, so it is a set.
The questions printed in this chapter are fixed and can be listed, so for any question one can decide definitely whether it belongs to the collection. It is well defined, so it is a set.
"Most dangerous" is not a definite criterion; different people will include different animals and there is no rule deciding membership. The collection is not well defined, so it is not a set.
The number \(5\) appears among the elements listed in \(A = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\), so it belongs to \(A\). Hence \(5 \in A\).
The number \(8\) is not one of the elements listed in \(A = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\), so it does not belong to \(A\). Hence \(8 \notin A\).
The number \(0\) is not one of the elements listed in \(A = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\), so it does not belong to \(A\). Hence \(0 \notin A\).
The number \(4\) appears among the elements listed in \(A = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\), so it belongs to \(A\). Hence \(4 \in A\).
The number \(2\) appears among the elements listed in \(A = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\), so it belongs to \(A\). Hence \(2 \in A\).
The number \(10\) is not one of the elements listed in \(A = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\), so it does not belong to \(A\). Hence \(10 \notin A\).
The integers \(x\) satisfying \(-3 \le x < 7\) are those from \(-3\) up to \(6\), the value \(7\) being excluded by the strict inequality. Listing them, \(A = \{-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\).
The natural numbers less than \(6\) are \(1, 2, 3, 4, 5\). Hence \(B = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}\).

Let the number be \(10t + u\) with tens digit \(t\) satisfying \(1 \le t \le 9\) and units digit \(u\) satisfying \(0 \le u \le 9\), and require \(t + u = 8\). Then \(u = 8 - t\) is a permissible digit exactly for \(t = 1, 2, \ldots, 8\) (while \(t = 9\) would give \(u = -1\)). This yields the numbers \(17, 26, 35, 44, 53, 62, 71, 80\), so \(C = \{17, 26, 35, 44, 53, 62, 71, 80\}\).
Factorising, \(60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5\), so the only primes dividing \(60\) are \(2\), \(3\) and \(5\). Hence \(D = \{2, 3, 5\}\).

The word TRIGONOMETRY has letters T, R, I, G, O, N, O, M, E, T, R, Y; in a set each element is written only once, so the repeated T, R and O are listed once each. Hence \(E = \{T, R, I, G, O, N, M, E, Y\}\).
The word BETTER has letters B, E, T, T, E, R; writing each distinct letter once gives \(F = \{B, E, T, R\}\).

Each listed element is a multiple of \(3\): \(3 = 3 \times 1\), \(6 = 3 \times 2\), \(9 = 3 \times 3\), \(12 = 3 \times 4\), and the list stops at \(12\). Hence the set is \(\{x : x = 3n,\ n \in \mathbf{N},\ 1 \le n \le 4\}\), that is, \(\{x : x \text{ is a multiple of } 3 \text{ and } x \le 12\}\).
_note: The stem is printed as "(3, 6, 9, 12}" — an opening round bracket against a closing brace. Solved as printed, reading it as the set {3, 6, 9, 12}, which is the only sensible reading.

solution: Each listed element is a power of \(2\): \(2 = 2^1\), \(4 = 2^2\), \(8 = 2^3\), \(16 = 2^4\), \(32 = 2^5\). Hence the set is \(\{x : x = 2^n,\ n \in \mathbf{N},\ 1 \le n \le 5\}\).
Each listed element is a power of \(5\): \(5 = 5^1\), \(25 = 5^2\), \(125 = 5^3\), \(625 = 5^4\). Hence the set is \(\{x : x = 5^n,\ n \in \mathbf{N},\ 1 \le n \le 4\}\).

The elements \(2, 4, 6, \ldots\) continue without end and are exactly the numbers of the form \(2n\) with \(n\) a natural number. Hence the set is \(\{x : x = 2n,\ n \in \mathbf{N}\}\), that is, \(\{x : x \text{ is an even natural number}\}\).
Each listed element is a perfect square: \(1 = 1^2\), \(4 = 2^2\), \(9 = 3^2\), and the list ends at \(100 = 10^2\). Hence the set is \(\{x : x = n^2,\ n \in \mathbf{N},\ 1 \le n \le 10\}\).

The odd natural numbers are those of the form \(2n - 1\) with \(n \in \mathbf{N}\), and there is no largest one, so the list never terminates. Hence \(A = \{1, 3, 5, 7, 9, \ldots\}\), an infinite set.
We need the integers \(x\) with \(-\frac{1}{2} < x < \frac{9}{2}\), i.e. \(-0.5 < x < 4.5\). The integers in this range are \(0, 1, 2, 3, 4\). Hence \(B = \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}\).
The condition \(x^2 \le 4\) means \(-2 \le x \le 2\), and \(x\) must be an integer. The integers satisfying this are \(-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\). Hence \(C = \{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\}\).
The word LOYAL uses the letters L, O, Y, A, L; the repeated L is written only once in a set. Hence \(D = \{L, O, Y, A\}\).

Of the twelve months, seven (January, March, May, July, August, October, December) have \(31\) days; the remaining months have \(30\) days, except February which has \(28\) or \(29\). Hence \(E = \{\text{February},\ \text{April},\ \text{June},\ \text{September},\ \text{November}\}\).
The letters preceding \(k\) in the English alphabet are \(a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j\). Removing the vowels \(a\), \(e\) and \(i\) leaves the consonants. Hence \(F = \{b, c, d, f, g, h, j\}\).

Write each set-builder description in roster form and compare. The natural numbers dividing \(6\) are \(1, 2, 3, 6\); of these the primes are \(2\) and \(3\); the odd natural numbers less than \(10\) are \(1, 3, 5, 7, 9\); and the distinct letters of MATHEMATICS are \(M, A, T, H, E, I, C, S\). Matching these against the rosters given, the pairing is \((\mathrm{i}) \leftrightarrow (\mathrm{c})\), \((\mathrm{ii}) \leftrightarrow (\mathrm{a})\), \((\mathrm{iii}) \leftrightarrow (\mathrm{d})\), \((\mathrm{iv}) \leftrightarrow (\mathrm{b})\).
A number divisible by \(2\) is even, so it cannot be odd; therefore no natural number is both odd and divisible by \(2\). The set has no element, so it is the null set.

The number \(2\) is prime and is even, so the set contains \(2\); in fact the set is exactly \(\{2\}\), since every other even number has \(2\) as a proper divisor and so is not prime. The set has an element, so it is not the null set.
The two conditions require \(x < 5\) and \(x > 7\) at the same time, which is impossible since no number is both less than \(5\) and greater than \(7\). The set has no element, so it is the null set.
Two lines in a plane are parallel precisely when they have no point in common, so there is no point lying on both. The set has no element, so it is the null set.
A year has exactly \(12\) months, so the elements can be counted and the counting comes to an end. The set is finite.
This is the set of all natural numbers; for every natural number \(n\) the number \(n + 1\) is also in the set, so the listing never ends. The set is infinite.
The elements are the natural numbers from \(1\) to \(100\), exactly \(100\) of them, so the counting comes to an end. The set is finite.
The set is \(\{101, 102, 103, \ldots\}\); for every such integer \(n\), the integer \(n + 1\) is again greater than \(100\), so the listing never ends. The set is infinite.

Every element is a natural number below \(99\), and there are only finitely many such numbers, so the primes among them can be listed and counted (they are \(2, 3, 5, \ldots, 97\)). The set is finite.
A line parallel to the \(x\)-axis has equation \(y = c\), and every real number \(c\) gives a different such line. Since there are infinitely many real numbers, the set is infinite.
The English alphabet has exactly \(26\) letters, so the elements can be counted and the counting comes to an end. The set is finite.
The multiples of \(5\) are \(5, 10, 15, 20, \ldots\), and for every multiple \(5n\) the number \(5(n+1)\) is again a multiple, so the listing never ends. The set is infinite.
At any given time the number of animals on the earth, though extremely large and hard to determine in practice, is a definite whole number. The set is finite.

A circle through the origin is determined by its centre \((h, k)\), its radius then being \(\sqrt{h^2 + k^2}\); every choice of centre other than the origin gives such a circle. Since there are infinitely many choices of \((h, k)\), the set is infinite.
Two sets are equal when they have exactly the same elements; the order in which the elements are written is irrelevant. Both sets contain precisely \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) and \(d\), so \(A = B\).

The positive even integers not exceeding \(10\) are \(2, 4, 6, 8, 10\), so in roster form \(B = \{2, 4, 6, 8, 10\}\). This is exactly the list given for \(A\), so \(A = B\).
In roster form \(A = \{10, 20, 30, 40, \ldots\}\), while \(B\) contains \(15\). Since \(15\) is not a multiple of \(10\), we have \(15 \in B\) but \(15 \notin A\), so \(A \ne B\).
Solve the equation: \(x^2 + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3) = 0\), so \(x = -2\) or \(x = -3\), giving \(B = \{-2, -3\}\). Since \(2 \in A\) but \(2 \notin B\), the sets are not equal, so \(A \ne B\).

The distinct letters of FOLLOW are \(F, O, L, W\), so \(A = \{F, O, L, W\}\); the distinct letters of WOLF are \(W, O, L, F\), so \(B = \{W, O, L, F\}\). Both sets have exactly the same elements, order being irrelevant, so \(A = B\).

Two sets are equal only if every element of each belongs to the other. Comparing the given sets: \(B = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\) and \(D = \{3, 1, 4, 2\}\) have exactly the same four elements, and \(E = \{-1, 1\}\) and \(G = \{1, -1\}\) have exactly the same two elements. No other pair matches: \(A\) and \(C\) differ because \(2 \in A\) while \(2 \notin C\) and \(14 \in C\) while \(14 \notin A\), and \(F = \{0, a\}\) differs from \(H = \{0, 1\}\) since \(a\) is not given to be \(1\). Hence the equal sets are \(B = D\) and \(E = G\).

Recall that \(A \subset B\) means every element of \(A\) is also an element of \(B\); to deny it, it is enough to exhibit one element of \(A\) that is not in \(B\). Here \(e \in A\) but \(e 
otin B\), since \(B\) consists only of \(a, b, c, d\); hence \(A\) is not a subset of \(B\). Similarly \(b \in B\) but \(b 
otin A\), since \(A\) consists only of the vowels \(a, e, i, o, u\); hence \(B\) is not a subset of \(A\). So \(A 
ot\subset B\) and \(B 
ot\subset A\); the two sets share only the element \(a\), and neither contains the other.
